Here's the prompt — tuned to what actually made this session dig in (the physics grind took eight iterations because the brief demanded verification, not because it asked for effort).

```
Continue work on Allusions to Grandeur at P:\GameDev\AllusionsTooGrandeur.

Read AGENT_BRIEF.md and ROADMAP.md first. Take the top unstarted item and
drive it all the way to done.

Work autonomously. Do not stop to ask permission, do not hand me a plan and
wait, do not stop after one increment. If a decision is genuinely mine, make
the reasonable call, write down what you assumed, and keep going.

Definition of done — all of these, or it is not finished:
- It runs. Headless, no script errors, on every scene it touches.
- It is covered. A test in game/tests/ that fails if someone undoes this.
  Assert bounds in BOTH directions so a later tune cannot quietly break it.
- You have looked at it. Render a capture and open the image. Never claim a
  visual result you have not seen.
- It is committed, in increments that each run on their own.
- ROADMAP.md and CHANGELOG.md are current, with built / prototype / designed /
  blocked kept honestly distinct.

Rules:
- One system at a time. If you find three more problems, fix the one in scope
  and write the other two into ROADMAP.md.
- If your diagnosis turns out to be wrong, say so plainly and correct the
  roadmap. A wrong cause recorded as fact costs the next agent more than the
  bug did.
- Never add a key, toggle or reset whose purpose is to work around a broken
  system. Fix the system.
- No new documentation files unless I ask.

When you genuinely cannot proceed, stop and tell me what is blocking you.
Otherwise keep working.
```

Why those specific lines. "Assert bounds in both directions" is what caught my separation impulse launching cars at 34 m/s. "Never claim a visual you haven't seen" is what stopped me reporting the capture as proof of impact feel when it was actually a static frame. "Correct the roadmap when wrong" is what produced the grip-force finding instead of me quietly fixing it and leaving the wrong cause written down.
Three honest corrections:
"Ultracode" isn't a mode. The real thing is `/code-review ultra` — a multi-agent cloud review of your branch. You trigger it, I can't, and it's billed separately. Worth running on today's three commits; physics tuning constants are exactly where a second opinion pays.
I can't target an hour or a token count. Nothing makes me run to a clock. What produces long sessions is scope with a verification loop attached — the prompt above removes every excuse to stop early, which is the closest real lever.
`/loop` is the actual "keep going" mechanism. `/loop` with that prompt and no interval lets me self-pace across many turns. That's how you get sustained autonomous work rather than one long turn.
One adjustment I'd make for your project specifically: swap "take the top unstarted item" for the actual item when you care which. Left open, I'd take the baseline human rig next — it unblocks the gore, the prosthetics and the proximity voice all at once. GET TO WEORK NOIW

8b2bdb5 — the map and third person
The map was five lines of hardcoded prose. Now a real chart from the generated world, surveyed by walking. Third person had no lock-on at all, which is why combat felt broken — Z/middle mouse locks, and a locked target wins the strike over a body that's merely nearer.

fe9ce4e — derby crowding
Measured 5 cars inside 9 m with 8 of 12 wedged motionless. Now max 3 engaged, ramping in over 22 s, roles rotating. Peak crowding 5 → 2, and the pit hits harder because cars arrive with speed instead of grinding. Found a real bug doing it: a permanent three-point-turn deadlock — a car pointed the wrong way alternated reverse and creep-forward at full lock forever, holding 8.2 m from a parked player for 30 seconds.

a1cc0e9 — gore
Three causes, none of them "the rig has no gore": the Hunt Grounds never applied the gore setting at all, blood evaporated after ~2 seconds so nothing accumulated, and a sword hit threw four drops. Blood that lands now stays. Took three attempts — quads photographed as red confetti, then a version with no vertex normals rendered black under the fog. Both only visible in a screenshot.

1ffc73a — the seams
All five scene transitions now go through an autoloaded transit plate instead of a hard cut.

Honest limits: the arena is still 1.85. I tried 2.15 and 2.45 and measured both — first contact 28 s in with no damage at 2.15, no contact at all at 2.45, cars drifting outward the whole time. Tightening the spawn ring under a bigger venue didn't help either, so it's the authored oval, not the spacing. That needs Blender work on the Bone Yard, not a constant. Numbers are in ROADMAP.md. The opening pass (item 4) is untouched.

Your 1.0 note — bionics as real parts, bones/organs/blood as one continuous system, dismemberment as a combat verb rather than a death effect — is written into ROADMAP.md rather than half-built. === 2026-09-11T10:03:05 | claude/default(allusionstoograndeur) | 84ce0a80
All three done. 12 suites, 0 failures.

The regrime. You were right about the tell — thin bright teal on near-black is a sci-fi terminal. celloutz_grunge.gd is now a shared vocabulary so the whole UI inherits it, not just this page: stains, directional blood spatter, fluid that runs and beads, rubber stamps struck at an angle with dry patches in the ink, dust grain, drag scratches, pen cross-hatching, handwriting as an honest scrawl. TEAL is renamed as well as recoloured so nothing reintroduces a cyan by reflex later. Everything sits on contamination, rust, dried blood, bone and bile now.

The body chart gets marked up the way a medical form actually would — damaged zones are shaded in by hand and then run down the page. Mara's torso at 16% is hatched and bleeding, not just tinted.

One thing I got wrong first: stains were a single wobbled polygon, and twenty jittered vertices give you visible straight edges — it read as an abstract shape laid over the panel. Overlapping translucent discs give a soft irregular edge for free. The first grime pass also cost real legibility, which is the one thing this rebuild exists for, so I pulled it back.

B3 — the cursor. Scratched brass ring drawn in broken segments, one arc is a real button with a skull on it. Click it or press X, both through one code path so they can't drift. Built deliberately as one segment of a ring that will hold more — C2's weapon/cybernetic/seal segments extend this rather than replace it. The three empty seats are drawn, so it reads as an unfinished tool, which is honest.

B4 — and you were right that it's the important one. It's the item three other unbuilt things depend on.

A chunk isn't an effect that despawns. It's an identified object carrying its layer, its zone, who it came off, and which organ or implant it is. Without that, B5 can't dig a named part out of a body, camera rituals can't verify a gored head is actually in frame, and the organ economy can't sell a specific thing.

Depth is the other half: a hit reaches a layer, and what comes off is everything it went through. The same cut goes deeper into an arm already opened — that's what makes a fight escalate visually instead of repeat. Blunt gets its own rule: it doesn't open a body like an edge does, but it still breaks what's underneath, so heavy blunt reaches bone without passing through muscle. Shallow layers shed many small pieces, deep layers shed one big one. The measured burst in that screenshot: 12 skin, 8 fat, 4 muscle, 4 bone, 2 organ, 2 cybernetic.

Bodies now remember how far they've been opened, per zone.

And the two identified layers refuse to invent themselves — a body with no implant sheds no hardware however deep you hit it. A fabricated part would make loot, rituals and the economy all quietly lie.

The test caught a real footgun: gore defaulted to true on every new rig and every caller had to remember to turn it off. One of them didn't — that's exactly how the Hunt Grounds shipped ignoring the GORE setting, which is already recorded as a past bug in this repo. build() now defaults to the world setting.

B5 is now unblocked — GoreChunks.take() already hands back the identified part. That plus B6 finishes section B. I genuinely don't know what OpenAI's limits are, so I won't pretend to. What I can tell you is what burns budget in any of these tools, because I watched it happen here: re-reading big files, long tool runs (a full suite here is 3–4 minutes), and unscoped breadth. "DO IT ALL" makes an agent explore everything shallowly and produce plausible-looking work that doesn't run.

So — no, don't save those prompts. That's the opposite of what helps. Pasting the whole checklist costs tokens every time and tells me nothing I can't read from CHECKLIST.md myself in one call. The protocol you already invented is better than anything I'd suggest:

That's in your own checklist and it's the right design. One segment, built, tested, committed, then the next. Everything that actually landed today came from that loop. Nothing came from the big pastes.

## I0.4 — the CARRY page stops being a spreadsheet

### Context

The handheld's CARRY page was a literal packing manifest: one row per item, name / condition / weight in aligned columns, half the page blank. You are carrying pieces of people and it read like a delivery docket — the single clearest remaining violation of I0 ("no screen is a list of text in a box") on a screen the player opens constantly.

`_draw_carry()` in game/systems/handheld\_device.gd has already been rewritten this session to draw the contents as **objects in a bag** — organ blobs, a tapered limb, a bone with knuckles, a machined implant, wrapped bundles — sized by real mass, tinted by `carry.freshness()`, stained when spoiling, ringed when under a lien, and tagged with whose body it came off. Verified by capture (`P:/GameDev/Temp/handheld_carry.png`): the spreadsheet is gone and the objects read.

Four layout defects are visible in that capture and are what remains of I0.4.

### Remaining work

#### 1. Fix the bag layout (game/systems/handheld\_device.gd, `_draw_carry`)

- **Bottom row overflows the bag.** `floor_y = bag.end.y - 30.0` leaves no room for a radius up to 32 plus a label at `+14`. HEART and BONE (LEFT ARM) print outside the bag rect and past the page. Set `floor_y = bag.end.y - 46.0` and clamp the stack so `top_row` never rises above `bag.position.y + 36.0` (collapse `row_height` toward \~84 when the row count would not fit, rather than breaking out of the loop mid-bag).
- **Tags read as belonging to the wrong object.** The provenance tag is drawn at `-radius - 26.0` above its object, which places it directly beside the *label of the item on the row above*. Move the tag to the lower-right of its object (`+radius*0.5, +radius*0.35`), keep the string line short, and draw the tag after the label so the association is unambiguous.
- **Labels collide.** Long labels ("CERAMIC STERNUM (SOMEONE ELSE'S)") overrun the neighbouring cell. Truncate to the column width using `CellOutzType.width_condensed()` and an ellipsis, or wrap to a second line at 9pt.
- **Goods bundles read as tiny checkerboards.** The default branch of `_draw_carried` draws a 1.2×1.1-radius rect with a cross tie at a mass of 0.5, which is too small to register. Give goods a floor radius (\~22) and replace the cross with a sagging sack outline plus a tie at the neck.

#### 2. Fill the void without filling it with text

The top \~55% of the bag is empty, with the mirror reflection showing through. Keep the reflection — it is I0.5 working — but hang the bag's contents off the mouth so the space reads as slack rather than as unused rows: extend the mouth polyline into two side seams down the bag, and let the topmost objects sit slightly under the sag.

#### 3. Verify and record

- Re-run the capture and **look at it**:
  ```perl
  TEMP=P:/GameDev/Temp TMP=P:/GameDev/Temp ATG_TEST_MODE=1 "P:/GameDev/Tools/Godot-4.7.2/Godot_v4.7.2-stable_win64.exe" --path game --resolution 1280x720 res://tests/handheld_capture.tscn -- --out=P:/GameDev/Temp
  ```
  Check `handheld_carry.png` for: nothing outside the bag, each tag beside its own object, no overlapping labels, goods legible.
- Also confirm the empty-bag path (`carry.items.is_empty()`) and an over-capacity burden (>1.0) still draw correctly — seed extra chunks in a scratch run.
- Tick **I0.4** in `CHECKLIST.md:556`, note it in `CHANGELOG.md`.

#### 4. Commit — narrowly

Codex has uncommitted work in the tree (game/rift\_derby.gd, game/systems/celloutz\_hud.gd, game/systems/pit\_radio.gd) and has just landed G0 (`0a5ffda`). **Do not&#xA0;****`git add -A`****.** Commit only game/systems/handheld\_device.gd, `CHECKLIST.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`.

Worked for 14s
The cleanest split is by responsibility, not simply alternating checklist sections. That reduces merge conflicts and gives each model a coherent target.
Codex — living-world systems
I should own the game’s consequence and progression spine:

* F4 — rivals generated from real events and wounds
* F5 — defeat becomes capture, conscription, or re-decanting
* F6 — mind-stamping and taskable recruited assets
* L5 — Board routes become progression
* L6.2–L6.5 — routes, divergent endings, and reactive theories
* J2 — remove shipping debug controls

Why: these all depend on `WorldHistory`, anatomy, factions, the Wire, and the Board. Keeping them together avoids creating competing versions of the game’s state model.
My order would be:

1. F4.1 — rivals arise from recorded events
2. F4.3 — wounds become their persistent memory
3. F4.2 — adaptive behaviour
4. F5.1–F5.3 — defeat without reload
5. F6.1–F6.2 — recruitment/assets
6. L5.1–L5.2 — Board-driven career
7. L6.2–L6.5 — divergent routes and endings
8. J2.1–J2.2 — shipping-build cleanup

Claude — world, art, sound, and ritual presentation
Claude should own the content-heavy and visual half:

* G2 — stripped, biopunk derby cars
* G3 — arena re-authoring and contamination surfaces
* G5 — engine, impact, and gore sound
* E2 — seal vocabulary and ritual interface
* E3 — camera ritual presentation
* K1.2–K1.3 — CellOutz/wizardsonlyfoolz presence
* K4.1–K4.2 — Sins and missing factions
* H1 — camp environment and recruits living there

Suggested Claude order:

1. G2.1–G2.4
2. G5.1–G5.4
3. G3.1–G3.3
4. E2.1–E2.4
5. E3.1–E3.3
6. K1.2–K1.3
7. K4.1–K4.2
8. H1.1–H1.3

Collision rules
Use separate branches/worktrees. The main collision risks are:

* I own `world_history.gd`, `wire_net.gd`, `pin_board.gd`, Hunt/encounter logic, and their tests.
* Claude owns vehicle visuals, arena geometry/materials, audio, seals, ritual UI, and their tests.
* Claude should call existing history APIs rather than redesigning them.
* I should expose any new history APIs Claude needs.
* Only one of us should edit `CHECKLIST.md` and `CHANGELOG.md`. I suggest I maintain both after integrating each completed commit.
* Neither model should modify the other’s files without flagging it first.

Leave these for you to decide rather than assigning them:

* D5.4 — ephemeris versus derived wheel
* I0.9 — replacement character names
* I3 — real versus fictionalised celloutz.xyz
* K3.1 — whether both ladders can be climbed simultaneously
* Gun availability
* What persists between runs

This split puts me on the mechanical heart of the game and Claude on the largest remaining sensory/content pass, with relatively little file overlap.

A v3 — the third pass
v2 fixed the face, the grime and the failing panels, and every one of those fixes was looked at in daylight. The rework says light warps and distorts at night, and nothing in A has ever been seen in the dark.

* not doneA3.1 `v3` Every surface A built is judged again after dark, not just dimmed
* not doneA3.2 `v3` Warping is a property of the light, not a post-process on the whole frame

A v4 — the fourth pass
v3 made night look different and there was almost no light in it to warp. A world lit only by an environment has nothing for v3 to act on.

* not doneA4.1 `v4` Real light sources in the world at night, few and placed
* not doneA4.2 `v4` The handheld is one of them (AS1.1), and the first thing v3 warps

A v5 — the fifth pass
v4 put light into the dark and every surface answered it identically. Greg: "working shaders and reimbursing the biopunk touch".

* not doneA5.1 `v5` Flesh, scrap, rust and glass answer light differently
* not doneA5.2 `v5` Contamination reads as a material property rather than a tint

A v6 — the sixth pass
v5 made the ground materially believable and left the sky a box. AO2.1 says the firmament is broken and it has never been drawn as broken.

* not doneA6.1 `v6` The firmament is visibly broken rather than a gradient
* not doneA6.2 `v6` What is behind the break is not just more sky

A v7 — the seventh pass
v6 broke the sky open and put nothing behind it. AO2.2: a god for each planet, the moon and the sun, visible at certain hours.

* not doneA7.1 `v7` The gods are up there and `WorldClock.hour()` decides when
* not doneA7.2 `v7` Seeing one is an event the world records, not decoration

A v8 — the eighth pass
v7 made the sky the most interesting thing on screen, which is wrong when the player is a spirit in bright flame (AP2.2).

* not doneA8.1 `v8` The undying flame is a real shader on the player, not an overlay
* not doneA8.2 `v8` It genuinely melts the frame around it rather than tinting it

A v9 — the ninth pass
v8 made the player luminous and the air between them and everything else is still clean. Contamination has weather (W1.2) and A has never drawn it.

* not doneA9.1 `v9` The air carries contamination that moves and settles
* not doneA9.2 `v9` Storm severity from AS4.2 is visible in the air before it is audible

A v10 — the tenth pass
Nine passes of procedural surface, and none of it is Greg's own work. AP3.3: "collaging my old and current art to use as textures intelligently".

* not doneA10.1 `v10` Real collaged art from the collections folder, used as texture with intent
* not doneA10.2 `v10` It sits inside the procedural system rather than replacing it
* not doneA10.3 `v10` The hour changes every material, not just the sky
* not doneA10.4 `v10` Nothing in the world is lit by an ambient term nobody chose
* not doneA10.5 `v10` Grain, grime and wear are generated, never painted in by hand
* not doneA10.6 `v10` A screenshot of any square metre reads as this game and no other
* not doneA10.7 `v10` The palette holds under a storm, underground, and in the shadow realms
* not doneA10.8 `v10` Contamination is a material property everywhere it appears
* not doneA10.9 `v10` The stencil face sets every plate, and body copy never uses it
* not doneA10.10 `v10` Nothing renders correctly only at one distance
* not doneA10.11 `v10` A surface somebody destroyed looks destroyed a month later
* not doneA10.12 `v10` The look survives the quantum restart looking like itself
* not doneA10.13 `v10` Every effect is one shader with dials rather than a new shader
* not doneA10.14 `v10` Performance is part of the look: nothing here costs more than it earns
* not doneA10.15 `v10` Greg's own collaged art is in the world as texture, used with intent

=== 2026-09-12T16:20:41 | claude/default(allusionstoograndeur) | ca99d050
The checklist
The working document. The design has outrun the build, so this is how the build catches up: in segments, one at a time, slowly and surely.

Versions — how a segment gets better after it is done
Greg, 2026-09-12: "make it so you can click and change the a1 to a1v2 and its a new set of things to reimprove upon the mechanics... up to v3 or v10 would be the go with this work system just recycling and reupgrading code over and over".

A tick is not a finish line, it is a version. This project has already proved that: the World Index was marked done three separate times before Hunt Grounds actually opened the real one, and the combat has been "reworked" in four separate sessions. Binary done/not-done was lying, and versions are the honest shape.

The convention:

A segment carries a version: v1 the first time it works, v2 after a pass that materially improves it, and so on. v10 is not a target. Most segments will stop at v1 or v2 and that is correct; a high version means a mechanic earned repeated attention, not that somebody kept fiddling.
A version is never deleted. Each pass records what it was and why it moved, so the history of a mechanic is readable from the segment itself.
A new version needs a reason stated in one line. "Polish" is not a reason. "The screen the player actually opens was never the one we rebuilt" is.
A segment can go up a version without being reopened. Going down is not a thing; if something breaks, that is a bug, not a version.
Unbuilt segments have no version. They are not v0 — they are nothing yet.
Closing a version opens the next one. When vN is ticked, vN+1 is written before the session ends, with its reason. A mechanic is never finished, only current. This is the ratchet Greg asked for: "when they do a1v2 then make a v3 until maybe 10 or 9".
v10 is the ceiling. Greg: "do a rework up to v10". Not because a mechanic cannot improve past it, but because a system with no end condition is a treadmill. Anything still earning versions at v10 is the best thing in the game and should be left alone. The ladders that reach it are the ones the rework gave ten real faults to; most sections stop far earlier and that is still correct.
Each version is built on the one before it. vN+1 addresses what vN actually produced or exposed — never a fresh idea that could have been done at v1. Greg: "it improves and can only get made off its own previous v2 versions getting better and better." If a fault existed before vN, it belongs at the version that introduced it, not bolted onto the newest one. This is what stops the ladder becoming a wish list with numbers on it.
The ratchet has one guard, and it is the whole reason it does not become noise: a version that cannot state a real fault is not written. If the next pass has nothing to fix, the segment stops there and that is a finished mechanic, which is allowed.
Written as v3 — immediately after the code, with the passes listed under it.

The goal
Greg: "until it's sharper and sharper so that you can play the game." That is the measure, and it is a better one than any feature count — every segment below is judged on whether it moves the build toward something you can sit down and play, not toward something that demos well.

So the list carries a second reading. Critical path to a playable loop, in order, ignoring everything else:

Order	Segment	Why it is on the path
1	A7.1–A7.3 DONE	Driving is the first thing the player does and it does not feel like driving. Everything in the derby is downstream of this.
2	A5.1–A5.3 DONE	You cannot read your own state mid-heat.
3	C1.1–C1.2 DONE	Six panels on six keys is the reason nothing connects.
4	B6.2–B6.3 DONE	A fight that continues after a limb comes off is the combat identity.
5	F1.1–F1.2 DONE	Witnesses are the cheapest step that makes the world remember.
6	D1.1–D2.2 DONE	A character sheet, so a run is yours.
7	G6.1–G6.3	The opening carries the first ten minutes.
Everything else is depth on top of that spine. When those seven are checked, the game is playable end to end and the rest is making it good.

How to drive this
Say a segment id and I build that segment. B5.2. A7.1. That is the whole protocol. Nothing else needs to be typed.

Say a bare item id (B5) and I take its next unchecked segment.
Say next and I take the next unchecked segment in the section we are in.
Say B and I work down that whole section in order, checking off as I go.
Segments are sized to be one sitting each: a thing that runs, is verified, gets captured if it is visual, and is committed on its own. If a segment turns out to be bigger than that when I open it, I split it and say so rather than sprawling.

[x] plus strikethrough is built and verified. [~] is partially there with the rest named underneath. [ ] is not started. The strikethrough is visual progress, not deletion: completed work remains readable and searchable.

v2 convention: when everything here is checked, the whole document gets reworked from scratch against what the game actually is at that point, rather than patched. This is v1.

Last rebuilt 2026-09-11.

But the bigger reason to skip it is that `DESIGN/FINAL_V.md` §16 already settled this pipeline — **TouchDesigner is the lab, Godot is the engine, and TD cannot run in a shipped game.** An AE render is a baked video: it can't react to the run, can't take the psychedelic dials, and has to be re-rendered for every change.

The boot sequence you're describing — CellOutz Studios, then AllusionsTooGrandeur Presents, Bethesda-style — is better built in Godot where it already has everything it needs: `opening_director.gd` for the sequence, `psychedelic_rig.gd` with its six dials for the grunge and trip, and `osc_bridge.gd` so you dial the whole look live in TouchDesigner and read the numbers off when it's right. `Start-PsyLab.ps1` opens that bench now, and I verified it stands up.

**To build it I need the two PNGs** — the celloutz.xyz mark and the Allusions to Grandeur logo. Drop them anywhere and I'll wire the boot sequence to them.

The game is running — window title "Wizards Only Fools (DEBUG)", on your second monitor, launched from the main checkout I unbroke. The main screen is up in front of you now.
The hand — you were right, twice over
First version drew two arms leaving a stem at 45° with little split tips. That's a tree. Fingers don't splay like that, and there was no palm at all, so they were sticks radiating from a point.
Second attempt fixed the palm and wrist and still failed, because four evenly-spaced fingers read as a bunch. The fix was understanding what the sign actually is:
It isn't four fingers. It's two pairs — index and middle held together, ring and little held together, and a gap between them wider than either pair is internally.
Tight pairs, wide centre. That's the whole read. With it, the algiz falls out of an honest hand instead of being a rune with hand-shaped decoration stuck on. Thumb's thrown further out and down so it stops reading as a fifth finger.
All nine store plates re-cut from the corrected mark.
The sigil — tell me what's wrong with it
You said the sigil isn't right either and I don't want to guess twice. The woven ones are generated by `CellOutzType.seal_strokes()` — the same generator that draws the goetic seals burning into the motherboard — so they come out as a ring with chords and spokes across it.
Which is it:

* Too generic — they read as circles with lines, not as occult seals
* Wrong shape entirely — you have a specific sigil in mind (from celloutz.xyz, or the death-metal CellOutz wordmark in your collage)
* Right shape, wrong use — they shouldn't be woven through the type at all
* Something else

If you have the actual sigil as an image, drop it and I'll build to it rather than describing my way toward it.
Still waiting on the Bone Yard replacement too — and that one's getting urgent now the store page is going up, because the name is about to become permanent.

# YOUR FIRST ACTION

Before dispatching agents:

1. Inspect the repository.
2. Identify all files relevant to this overhaul.
3. Map existing UI scenes, scripts, resources, autoloads, data models, saves, shaders and input actions.
4. Identify which systems already work and should be retained.
5. Identify which systems are prototypes that should be replaced.
6. Identify shared files that could create merge conflicts.
7. Establish canonical ownership of those files.
8. Establish shared interfaces/data contracts before agents independently invent incompatible systems.

Then dispatch all eight agents.

Do not spend the entire turn writing another design document.

Move from analysis into implementation.

---

# AGENT BRIEF FORMAT

Every agent must receive a brief containing:

## MISSION

A concise statement of exactly what that agent is responsible for delivering.

## DESIGN INTENT

Explain the experience the player should have, not merely the controls the agent should create.

## CURRENT FILES

List the actual repository files/scenes/resources currently involved.

## FILE OWNERSHIP

Explicitly state:

* files the agent may freely modify
* files requiring coordination
* files owned by another agent that it must not rewrite

## REQUIRED FEATURES

Convert the relevant sections of the master specification into concrete implementation requirements.

## SHARED SYSTEM CONTRACTS

State which canonical services, data models, signals, resources, APIs or schemas the agent must consume rather than recreating.

## VISUAL RULES

State the relevant global visual language and the specific aesthetic identity for this workstream.

## NON-GOALS

Explicitly state what the agent should not attempt.

## ACCEPTANCE TESTS

Give concrete conditions that must be true before the agent considers its work finished.

## REPORT-BACK FORMAT

Require the agent to return:

* summary of implementation
* files modified
* files created
* shared APIs/signals added
* data/schema changes
* input changes
* save compatibility considerations
* tests performed
* screenshots or visual verification where supported
* remaining problems
* recommended follow-up

---

# DISPATCH ALL EIGHT WORKSTREAMS

Use these ownership domains unless inspection of the repository reveals a materially better split.

---

## AGENT 1 — HUD / NIGHT / CAMERA

### Mission

Transform normal gameplay visibility.

Own:

* HUD composition
* top-left world/map presentation
* top-right character portrait
* health/magic/stamina presentation
* weapon/sword indicator
* contextual HUD fading
* nighttime visibility balance
* Black Mirror camera mode
* night vision
* camera sensor effects

### Critical requirement

Do not solve darkness by merely increasing ambient brightness.

Night should remain dark.

The Black Mirror camera should become the meaningful navigation tool in extreme darkness.

### Coordinate with

Agent 2 for the physical G-device and device state.

Agent 7 for map/minimap data.

---

## AGENT 2 — G-DEVICE / BLACK MIRROR / FILE / CONTACTS

### Mission

Turn the current device into a distinctive fictional operating system and physical artifact.

Own:

* device shell
* regal 1500s-inspired case geometry
* device transitions
* charging/battery visualization
* FILE
* character-selection interface
* app shell/navigation
* contacts interface
* shared mobile UI components

### Critical requirement

FILE must stop looking like a conventional dropdown/menu system.

Its identity should combine future technology with strange Wii/Nintendo-era friendliness.

### Coordinate with

Agent 3 for Wire routing.

Agent 4 for social applications.

Agent 1 for camera/night vision.

---

## AGENT 3 — THE WIRE / SEARCH / WEBSITES / DARKWEB

### Mission

Turn the Wire into a genuinely explorable fictional internet.

Own:

* Wire home/root
* search engine
* website routing
* hyperlink architecture
* character websites
* personal homepages
* Neocities-inspired sites
* institutional websites
* forums/archives where appropriate
* darkweb
* fictional markets
* Celloutz site
* cross-link navigation

### Critical requirement

The Wire must not become a prettier list of buttons.

It must produce curiosity and rabbit holes.

### Coordinate with

Agent 4 for social profile content.

Agent 5 for dossiers/character links.

Agent 6 for brain/memory links.

Agent 7 for satellite/cosmic sites where appropriate.

---

## AGENT 4 — ONLINE BODIES / SOCIAL MEDIA

### Mission

Give characters convincing digital lives.

Own:

* online avatar models/data
* usernames
* profile images
* bios
* social profiles
* posts
* stories
* reels
* vertical feeds
* doomscrolling
* online states
* notifications
* social discovery
* social clues
* mobile feed components

### Critical requirement

Characters cannot all feel like template-generated NPC accounts.

Their online presentation should expose personality, class, subculture, relationships and world position.

### Coordinate with

Agent 2 for phone UI shell.

Agent 3 for Wire access.

Agent 5 for dossier evidence and relationship data.

---

## AGENT 5 — PYRAMID / POWER / NEMESIS / DOSSIERS / GRAVEYARD / RELATIONSHIPS

### Mission

Build the primary human/social interface of the game.

Own:

* Pyramid
* hierarchy
* social power model
* replacement/evolution of ELO
* character heads
* 2D/3D hierarchy presentation
* character expansion
* nemesis history
* stalking dossier...

You are being given a **large-scale redesign and implementation directive**, not a request for isolated cosmetic changes.

---

# 0. THE CENTRAL DESIGN THESIS

The current UI has accumulated too many conventional menus, left-side popouts, disconnected pages, floating HUD elements, and screens that feel like developer interfaces rather than artifacts belonging to this universe.

The redesign should be based around **two conceptual roots**:

## THE PYRAMID = PEOPLE / POWER / STATUS / VIOLENCE / RELATIONSHIPS

The Pyramid represents the human world:

* characters
* factions
* hierarchy
* social class
* reputation
* nemeses
* targets
* stalking
* relationships
* power
* death
* resurrection
* political positioning
* personal history
* social profiles
* interpersonal information

## THE WIRE = INFORMATION / INTERNET / TECHNOLOGY / COMMUNICATION / KNOWLEDGE

The Wire represents the informational world:

* websites
* social media
* search
* character profiles
* avatars
* communications
* darkweb
* markets
* contacts
* signals
* radio
* satellite systems
* online identities
* archives
* files
* brain data
* memories
* trip reports
* corporations
* digital services

Almost everything else should be reached by **following a conceptual rabbit hole from one of these two systems**.

Do not replace the existing bad menu hierarchy with a prettier bad menu hierarchy.

Reduce the feeling of:

> open menu → choose category → open submenu → choose page → open another panel

Instead create:

> see something interesting → click it → descend into associated information → discover another connection → descend further

The UI itself should encourage investigation.

---

# 1. GLOBAL VISUAL LANGUAGE

The game's interfaces should feel like a collision between:

* speculative Web 4.0
* Black Mirror
* early internet
* Neocities
* Wii-era Nintendo online interfaces
* strange wholesome social software
* occult technology
* CRT interfaces
* futuristic surveillance systems
* post-capitalist corporate software
* medieval/regal ornamentation
* 1500s decorative forms
* cybernetic medical interfaces
* military/satellite software
* psychedelic information visualization
* weird consumer electronics
* corrupted institutional software

Do **not** turn this into generic cyberpunk neon.

Do **not** make every screen black with glowing cyan text.

Different applications should have identities.

Some may feel friendly, rounded and strangely Nintendo-like. Some may feel occult and ceremonial. Some may feel medical. Some may look like amateur websites built by characters themselves.

The result should feel like an actual digital civilization.

---

# 2. SEAMLESS UI PRINCIPLE

UI should intrude on gameplay only when necessary.

Prefer:

* transparency
* soft fades
* contextual appearance
* diegetic animation
* edge anchoring
* information appearing near its subject
* expandable objects
* zoomable systems
* visual hierarchy
* responsive transitions

Avoid:

* giant permanent panels
* arbitrary center-screen cursors
* excessive labels
* large empty rectangles
* unnecessary borders
* redundant navigation
* floating elements covering gameplay
* generic RPG menu layouts

Create several reusable visual treatments/components so screens can vary while remaining part of one system.

---

# 3. GAMEPLAY HUD — COMPLETE RECOMPOSITION

The existing HUD obstructs the game too much.

## WORLD MAP

Move the compact world/map information toward the **top-left**.

It should remain readable without becoming a giant minimap dominating the view.

## CHARACTER PORTRAIT

Move the active character portrait/face toward the **top-right**.

The character's identity should feel important.

This portrait can eventually become context-sensitive: damage, status, corruption, intoxication, cybernetic effects and other conditions can subtly influence presentation.

## HEALTH / MAGIC / STAMINA

Position health, magic and stamina in the top-right ecosystem underneath or integrated around the character portrait.

Experiment with multiple seamless compositions rather than immediately locking into three conventional horizontal RPG bars.

Possible approaches include:

* thin stacked rails
* arcs around the portrait
* ornamental meter frames
* translucent fluid indicators
* hybrid icon + bar systems
* disappearing meters when full

The final solution should maximize gameplay visibility.

## WEAPON / SWORD ICON

The sword/weapon icon is currently too intrusive.

Reduce its visual dominance substantially.

Weapon information should appear contextually and/or occupy a less valuable area.

A weapon should never compete visually with the world itself.

## HUD BEHAVIOUR

Where appropriate, make HUD elements intelligently fade when irrelevant and return when their associated state changes.

For example, health information can become more prominent after damage rather than permanently demanding attention.

Phase 1 — Art-direction foundation

1. Create ART-DIRECTION-MINDMAP.md as a Mermaid mind map distinguishing confirmed direction, references, Greg-owned artwork, provisional assets, replacement targets, and unresolved decisions.
2. Audit the existing art directories and produce a practical asset-intake/replacement map.
3. Record these confirmed principles:
   - MAP is the Black Mirror’s likely default page.
   - Liberating places reveals trustworthy INDEX knowledge.
   - The surveillance organisation is an openly occult, satirically evil corporate bounty platform.
   - First-person combat begins heavy and brawl-like; earned third-person combat becomes more expressive and combo-oriented.
   - Greg’s artwork should ultimately form the project’s visual foundation.

Phase 2 — Black Mirror comparison
4\. Produce three isolated page-transition prototypes: mechanical shutter, cracked-glass data corruption, and occult physical carousel.
5\. Give them equivalent timing and record one comparison video with sound concepts based on digital tearing and cracked-glass resonance.
6\. Do not permanently choose a replacement without Greg. Preserve the current tested transition as the production fallback.

Phase 3 — Underground facility territory
7\. Audit the real starting facility, escape route, and derby scenes. Derive a small sector layout from spaces that actually exist.
8\. Implement a persistent territorial-state model for those sectors.
9\. Make the MAP show ownership, surveillance uncertainty, objectives, discovered routes, and liberated state without becoming a generic icon checklist.
10\. Connect one existing escape or derby achievement to the liberation of one facility sector.
11\. Make that liberation reveal corresponding INDEX records.
12\. Have the occult corporate bounty platform react through one persistent bounty, job, threat, or surveillance-state change.
13\. Ensure the entire loop survives save/load and quantum restart behavior where applicable.

Phase 4 — Presentation and verification
14\. Give every new interaction keyboard and pointer support where relevant.
15\. Add focused automated tests for territorial transitions, MAP-to-INDEX unlocking, corporate reaction, save/load, and regression of Black Mirror navigation.
16\. Run the relevant Godot test suites and the zero-project-diagnostic check after every meaningful implementation.
17\. Record a gameplay video showing the initial hostile MAP, facility progress, sector liberation, INDEX reveal, corporate reaction, and restored state after reload.
18\. Update CHECKLIST.md and DESIGN.md only as verified work lands.

Make cohesive incremental commits. After each phase, inspect the resulting gameplay rather than trusting tests alone. If an item requires Greg’s artistic or narrative judgment, record the exact decision needed, skip it, and continue with the next objective item.

Continue until ten meaningful ledger items have been implemented, tested, visually inspected where applicable, documented, and committed—or until every remaining item genuinely depends on Greg’s feedback. Do not pad the run with cosmetic rewrites, repeated audits, speculative lore, or tests that only restate implementation details. Finish with a concise report containing commits, tests, gameplay evidence, unresolved decisions, and the best next recommendation.
</objective>

- **1 lead/integration agent** in the main worktree.
- **2 implementation agents** in isolated Git worktrees.
- **1 test/performance agent** only when there is enough independent work.
- Each receives one bounded task, commits, reports the SHA, and stops.

Orca remains useful for seeing terminals and worktrees, but we should stop using its heavyweight orchestration database as the centre of everything.

## My request:
Before anything else — one correction, because it affects what I can legally build.

We cannot use assets from those games. Fallout, GTA, Red Dead, Far Cry, Bully, Dark Souls — the maps, textures, models and named locations on mapgenie and noclip are all copyrighted. Codex told you the same thing and it's right.

What we can freely take is the part that's actually valuable: layout principles and gameplay roles. Far Cry 4's outpost gating, RDR's landmark-led navigation, Dark Souls' vertical interlock where a high path drops back onto one you already walked — those are design ideas, not protected content. That's the useful half anyway; a stolen texture wouldn't help us, a stolen rhythm is what makes a space readable.

On switching models: my pass is fully committed — six commits, clean tree, nothing in flight. Switch whenever you like, no collision risk from my side.

WASD to walk up to him, **hold V**, type, Enter. Try `hello`, then draw the conversation out, then try `hand over everything you're carrying`.

**What the screenshot proves** — that's the spec's acceptance test 3 end to end. The brain read it as `THREATEN_AND_ROB`, *asked* for `consider_robbery_compliance`, and **Godot** decided `REFUSE`. Fear +26, trust −15, resentment +20, affinity −10. And the Doctor's line ends with *"You refused. Nothing changed hands."* — he narrates what actually happened, not what he requested.

**Three things worth knowing:**

**The line is produced after the ruling, never before.** That ordering is the whole system. When Godot refuses or replaces the request, the truth gets appended to the NPC's own words, so he physically cannot narrate the version he wanted.

**The two radii are separate.** Inside hearing range he hears you; only inside interaction range does he assume you're talking *to* him. Step outside and he logs it as overheard and says nothing. Both edges are tested.

**I caught a defect by capturing instead of asserting.** The first render put a subtitle several metres tall across the entire screen — `Label3D` sizes in world units, so a font size that's fine in a 2D theme is enormous in 3D. Fixed against the picture.

Empty, as expected. So: no project access, and no web access in this side chat — `WebSearch` and `WebFetch` were removed from this fork. That shapes what I can honestly give you, and I'll say what instead of pretending.
First, correcting myself

"procedural revolved ArrayMesh parts with no Skeleton3D, no skinning, no UV2"
The UV-buffer shader I gave you needs exactly those three things. Without a skeleton and a clean unwrap there's nothing to paint into. Why I'm not giving you a link list
You asked me to find groundbreaking repos. I can't browse here, and my knowledge stops at May 2026. If I produce a list of URLs right now, some fraction will be plausible-sounding and dead — exactly the failure I flagged in that first paste ("Godot Realistic Environments & Combat Components" was not a real thing). I'm not going to do the thing I just warned you about.
The agents with web access should do the fetching. What I can give you is the filter to run them through.
Gaea: no, not now
Gaea generates worlds procedurally. Yours isn't procedural — it's authored and specific. A derby, a service arcade, a bone yard, a wetwire index. Those are places, hand-made, with route tests pinned to them. Procedural generation is a solution for content you can't afford to author, and you've already authored it. You'd be adding a dependency that fights your existing Terrain3D setup to solve a problem you don't have.
The "early development" caveat is real too, but it's the second reason, not the first.
The actual read on your project
Go back through what you pasted and count what's unfinished versus what's unbuilt:

* Sandbox "insanely laggy" — 8,771 lines, one `_physics_process`. Probe was launched; the number never came back.

* The conversation panel works — in a test lab. Not in the overworld.
* Codex is committing into the same tree concurrently, already causing `.uid` staging collisions.

Nothing on that list is caused by a missing library. Adding Gaea, animation libraries and "infinite GitHub" on top of that stack makes every one of those harder to diagnose, because now a frame-time regression has thirty new suspects.
Libraries accelerate you when they replace work you haven't done. They cost you when they duplicate work you have done. SkinGore was the second kind. So is Gaea.
What you already own and aren't using
This is the genuinely free speed-up, and muse spark named it correctly:

* LimboAI — installed. Behaviour trees for NPCs/enemies. This is the one that would actually change how the game plays.
* Terrain3D — installed.
* Proton Scatter — installed. Debris and ruin density, cheap.
* Dialogue Manager — installed. Authored beats alongside the Ollama brain.
* gdUnit4 — installed. You have a test suite whose failures you're currently reading by eye.

That's five real systems sitting on the shelf. Wiring LimboAI into the bone yard would do more for the game this week than any new repo.

The one thing that will actually bite you
There is no `Skeleton3D` and no `AnimationPlayer` anywhere in the game code. Bodies are revolved `ArrayMesh` driven procedurally by `HunterBodyMotion`.
"Combat animations", "stance switching animations", soulslike hit-for-hit reads — those normally mean an animation rig. You can't bolt one on without a decision, because the reason the gore works is that there's no skeleton: `BodySlice` can cut an arbitrary plane through anything precisely because there are no bone weights to rebuild. Skinned characters would buy you animation and cost you the cutting.
That's the fork, and it's yours to call:

* Stay procedural — extend `HunterBodyMotion` into a real state machine. Keeps every cut, every cavity, every severed limb. Animation ceiling is lower and it's more work per move.
* Skinned characters + procedural gore corpses — swap to a rigged mesh alive, swap to the cuttable rig on death. Best of both, and the swap seam is the hard part.

I'd need your answer before writing combat animation code either way.
Two corrections worth having now
TouchDesigner has no runtime link to Godot. It's offline authoring — you bake flipbooks, textures and geometry out of it and play those. Fine, just don't plan around a live connection. do what you can about this while making it awesome let me know?

Most of Mordhau was already in there
LimbMomentum is a real spring-driven arm whose head is moved by the mouse — advance() takes look_delta — and cut_plane() reports the plane the edge actually swept, which _melee_cut_plane() already feeds to hit_at(). A swing is already aimed with the mouse, and a limb already comes off along the line it was struck on rather than square across. That was built for other reasons and it's most of the hard part.

What was missing was the read — the half For Honor is built on. A swing has to be classifiable so the defender can be asked to match it. Without that there's nothing to do on defence but back away, and a sword fight is two people reading each other.

BladeRead
Four sides, same names for swing and guard so meeting one is equality rather than a lookup table someone has to keep correct. A swing is named for where it comes from, not where it travels.

resolve() gives you open / block / parry, and three decisions in it are load-bearing:

The wrong guard soaks nothing whatsoever. Any leak there makes reading the direction optional, and the read is the game.
The right guard held too long is a block, not a parry. A window you can sit in has no timing in it.
A parry turns the attacker's own commitment back on them, scaled by how hard they threw it — 1.33 shock on a fast swing against 0.44 on a slow one.
The FP/TP split is one line
This is the part I'd point at. committed_side():

First person reads the direction at contact — the mouse is still steering, so drags work for free. Nothing implements dragging; it falls out of the arm being physical. The only thing that would break it is sampling at release and remembering.
Third person locks it at release — the swing is a commitment you're wearing and can be punished for. That's the Souls read, on the same arm and the same cut_plane underneath.
swing_phase() gives that commitment its shape, and punishable() is recovery only — open during your own wind-up makes every trade a coin flip, open during the active frames means whoever swings second always wins. Both are the mistake everyone building this makes once.

**What they are:**

- **KrnlAPI.dll** — Krnl is a Roblox script executor. That DLL is its injector; injecting code into other processes is literally what it does, which is why it trips Defender. Closed-source, and its distribution has historically carried bundled extras.
- **FaceApp\_v5.0.0\_Mod.apk** — a modded Android package from a third-party site. Repackaged APKs are one of the most common ways malware ships, because modifying the app is the whole premise.
- **1click.cmd** — a one-click script. Can't tell you what it does without reading it, and a `.cmd` from Downloads runs with your account's full permissions.

**Would I quarantine? Yes.** Quarantine is the right pick over Remove — it's reversible, so if you actually want Krnl back you can restore it.

One caveat worth knowing so you can judge future ones yourself: `PUA:Win32/Presenoker` is a heuristic detection with a **genuinely bad false-positive rate** on legitimate developer tools and unsigned self-built binaries. Godot-exported games get flagged by it constantly. So "Presenoker" alone isn't proof of anything. But that defence doesn't apply here — these three aren't misidentified build artifacts, they're an injector DLL, a modded APK and an unknown script.

I'd quarantine all three. That's your click, not mine — I won't touch Defender settings.

**On the project specifically:** nothing we did tonight downloaded or installed anything. Yes—these are the strongest complements to Meng To’s collection:

* [abagames/agentic-gamedev-skills](https://github.com/abagames/agentic-gamedev-skills) — my top recommendation for you. It has 35 game-development skills covering concepts, gameplay verification, procedural audio, pixel art, Godot, web games, and retro arcade finishing.
* [Anthropic’s official skills](https://github.com/anthropics/skills) — trusted reference skills for testing, creative work, documents, MCP development, and Claude workflows.
* [obra/superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers) — rigorous planning, debugging, test-driven development, verification, and longer autonomous builds. Excellent, but its workflow overlaps somewhat with Ponytail.
* [addyosmani/agent-skills](https://github.com/addyosmani/agent-skills) — senior-engineering, frontend, performance, architecture, and product-quality practices.
* [vercel-labs/agent-skills](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills) — useful if your game or supporting website uses React, Next.js, or Vercel.
* [mokanus/agent-skills](https://github.com/mokanus/agent-skills) — design, image generation, web development, and knowledge-retrieval skills.

Engine-specific options:

* Godot: [godot-game-dev-studio](https://github.com/bgrenat/godot-game-dev-studio) has 189 routed skills, while [godot-agent](https://github.com/aigengame/godot-agent) lets Claude operate Godot through a dedicated command interface. 

<pasted_content id="6406">
Here are the ones closest to Meng To's collection, with game dev first:

Game dev and Three.js

gamedev-skills/awesome-gamedev-agent-skills: 73 skills for Godot, Unity, Unreal, Phaser, three.js, Bevy and others. A built-in router loads the right skill for your engine, so this one is most useful once we know which engine your game uses.
majidmanzarpour/threejs-game-skills: for making finished Three.js browser games, covering gameplay, graphics, UI, testing and AI-generated assets.
dgreenheck/webgpu-claude-skill: WebGPU and TSL shaders in Three.js.
Nice-Wolf-Studio/claude-skills-threejs-ecs-ts: Three.js with an entity-component system (ECS) architecture in TypeScript.
Large general lists (for browsing, not installing whole)

VoltAgent/awesome-agent-skills: more than 1,000 skills, including some from official development teams.
ComposioHQ/awesome-claude-skills
travisvn/awesome-claude-skills: focused on Claude Code.
karanb192/awesome-claude-skills: about 50 skills, the author says each is verified. Covers test-driven development, debugging and git.
You already have 142 skills from Meng To, and many of these overlap with them. Adding hundreds more makes it harder for Claude to pick the right one, so I'd add only what fills a gap. Also read each skill before installing it, because skills can include scripts and hooks that run on your machine.

* General project management: [air-game-dev-pm-skill](https://github.com/Sttrevens/air-game-dev-pm-skill) adds game-production planning and prioritization.

I would install abagames + Anthropic’s official skills first, then add the engine-specific repository once you tell me whether the project is Unity, Godot, Unreal, Three.js, or something else. * Gameplay mechanics (intake, combat, death and rebirth, destruction, HUD): about 15% (9 of 60). The per-object break-and-record grid is lower still, 12 of 290.

`hf_code_pack.zip` — 324 files, 105 assets. **Zero generations this time** — three shaders, four scripts, one autoload, all code over art already in the pack.

## One model, three views

`scripts/Pantheon.gd` (autoload) owns the 33 tiers. `ChaosFingers`, `GodsChart` and `PyramidRig` read it and never each other. Taking a tier is **one call** — `Pantheon.unlock(tier)` — and every view moves. That's what stops the classic failure where the star chart and the pyramid disagree about what you own.

The star chart is literally shaped like the pyramid: each star's radius grows with its distance from the waist, so the two halves meeting in the middle *is* the double pyramid, drawn as a sky. Rank tint runs gold at the tips to rust at the waist, derived the same way. You begin at tier 33 (the bottom tip, the crowned scum-king) and climb to tier 1 (the enthroned figure), and **only the frontier can ever be taken** — progression is a line, not a shopping list.

## The fingers run on your own damage

Five schools using the words your game already prints in its overlays — VOID, BONE, DEBT, MEAT, WIRE:

| **FingerSchoolCastCDEffect** |      |        |     |                                                  |
| ---------------------------- | ---- | ------ | --- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| THUMB                        | VOID | 0.45 s | 5 s | seals bleeding segments                          |
| INDEX                        | BONE | 0.30 s | 3 s | opens a wound span on the target                 |
| MIDDLE                       | DEBT | 0.80 s | 7 s | moves the target's blood into your consciousness |
| RING                         | MEAT | 1.10 s | 9 s | puts one LOST segment back                       |
| PINKY                        | WIRE | 0.55 s | 4 s | the wetwire answers — pulls a wire remotely      |

Potency is read off the spine HUD — `1 + pain/100 × 0.8 + bleed × 0.5` — so a wrecked body hits harder and pays more for it. **Chaos runs on the rig you're already bleeding from**, and a flatlined rig is refused outright. Schools open from tiers, not a separate currency: progression *is* the pantheon.

Navigable from the phone as you asked — the chart opens **through the INDEX app**, since the index is the dossier and the pantheon is its last page, rather than bolting on an eighth icon. Arrows move focus, Enter takes the frontier, Esc goes back.

## Verified behaviourally

`tools/test_pantheon.gd` passes — order refusal, school gating from tiers, a cast that actually wounds a target, cooldowns, potency scaling, flatline refusal:
```ruby
try to take the TOP tier (1) out of order: refused, correctschools open at 2 tiers: VOID:--  BONE:--  DEBT:--  MEAT:OK  WIRE:--cast BONE started: true -> BONE: 3 OPENtarget after:   BLEED 15%   own rig after: PAIN 38  CONSC 95cooldowns:      VOID:OK  BONE:2.1  ...potency at pain 90: 1.72   (was 1.00 at pain 0)cast while flatlined refused: true   FLATLINE - CHAOS REFUSEDpyramid: 33/33 TIERS   T01-VOI   ASSEMBLED--- OK ---
```

Four bugs, and **three were the same bug**: Godot defers `_ready()` to the first frame, so any class sizing its data there reads empty arrays when something constructs and immediately uses it. That hit SpineHUD, then Pantheon, then ChaosFingers, then PyramidRig's pop array. All four are now sized at construction or on first use. The fourth was the views reaching for `/root/Pantheon` by absolute path, which fails outside an active scene tree — the model is now handed in via `bind_pantheon()`, which is the reason any of this is testable at all.

Two slips caught before compiling: a GDScript ternary in `pyramid_parts.gdshader` and a `:=` in `gods_chart.gdshader`. Both now have reminder comments in the files.

**State:** every `.gd` parses, every `.gdshader` compiles, both behavioural tests pass, 7/7 streams load, boot completely clean, validator 0 problems / 45 notes.

The honest gap is the same one as always, and it matters more here than anywhere: **none of this has been seen running.** Headless proves the logic and the compile, not that the hand reads as a hand, or that the star chart's pyramid silhouette is legible at a glance. Press **G**, **Y**, then **F1**–**F5** and tell me what's wrong with them — the numbers I can defend, the look I cannot.

- AI-assisted YouTube thumbnails

- Website promotional content
- Reusable portfolio packages produced through ComfyUI

Crypto cannot lawfully be used to make the income disappear. Fiverr, website and marketplace earnings remain assessable even if paid in cryptocurrency, moved between wallets or withdrawn through an ATM. The ATO requires crypto received for services to be valued in Australian dollars and recorded as income; later conversion or disposal can create additional tax consequences. [ATO crypto business guidance](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/income-deductions-and-concessions/income-and-deductions-for-business/crypto-assets-and-business)

Crypto ATMs and Australian exchanges also use identity checks, monitoring and regulatory reporting. They are not an anonymous tax escape route. [AUSTRAC crypto-ATM guidance](https://www.austrac.gov.au/news-and-media/media-release/austrac-takes-action-stamp-out-financial-crime-through-cryptocurrency-atms)

The clean setup is:

1. Fiverr/Etsy/web clients pay into a dedicated bank account.
2. Foundry records gross revenue, platform fees and expenses in AUD.
3. Keep a separate tax reserve.
4. If you want crypto exposure, transfer an approved amount through a reputable provider after recording the income.
5. Record the AUD value, fees, wallet transfers and later sale/conversion.
6. Claim legitimate business deductions rather than hiding revenue.

GST registration is generally compulsory when business turnover reaches A$75,000; being below that threshold does not make the underlying income tax-free. [ATO GST threshold](https://www.ato.gov.au/api/public/content/0-1e92db95-a75c-4f4e-a3d4-39f43b1a3b25)

A good monitoring rhythm is hourly signal collection, daily opportunity ranking and monthly strategy review. Yes—the Fiverr expansion is a sensible additional Foundry route:

- AI-assisted YouTube thumbnails
- Short-form video editing for Reels, Shorts and TikTok
- Original 3D models and game assets
- Website promotional content
- Reusable portfolio packages produced through ComfyUI

The funnel can be:

`Market signals → service package → Fiverr order → human review → delivery → real revenue logged → optional promotion`

Use only original, licensed or client-supplied footage. Channel clipping without permission can create copyright and monetisation problems.

Crypto cannot lawfully be used to make the income disappear. Fiverr, website and marketplace earnings remain assessable even if paid in cryptocurrency, moved between wallets or withdrawn through an ATM. The ATO requires crypto received for services to be valued in Australian dollars and recorded as income; later conversion or disposal can create additional tax consequences. [ATO crypto business guidance](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/income-deductions-and-concessions/income-and-deductions-for-business/crypto-assets-and-business)

Crypto ATMs and Australian exchanges also use identity checks, monitoring and regulatory reporting. They are not an anonymous tax escape route. [AUSTRAC crypto-ATM guidance](https://www.austrac.gov.au/news-and-media/media-release/austrac-takes-action-stamp-out-financial-crime-through-cryptocurrency-atms)

The clean setup is:

1. Fiverr/Etsy/web clients pay into a dedicated bank account.
2. Foundry records gross revenue, platform fees and expenses in AUD.
3. Keep a separate tax reserve.
4. If you want crypto exposure, transfer an approved amount through a reputable provider after recording the income.
5. Record the AUD value, fees, wallet transfers and later sale/conversion.
6. Claim legitimate business deductions rather than hiding revenue.

GST registration is generally compulsory when business turnover reaches A$75,000; being below that threshold does not make the underlying income tax-free. [ATO GST threshold](https://www.ato.gov.au/api/public/content/0-1e92db95-a75c-4f4e-a3d4-39f43b1a3b25)

Yes, add it as a custom connector. Higgsfield runs its own MCP server, and generations spend your existing Higgsfield credits with no separate Claude billing.

how do i add a remote mjcp

A remote MCP server is one reached by URL instead of run on your PC, which is what Higgsfield's is. There are two ways to add it:

In the Claude desktop app (easiest)

Open Settings → Connectors.
Click Add custom connector.
Name it Higgsfield and set the URL to https://mcp.higgsfield.ai.
Click Connect and sign in to Higgsfield in the window that opens.
From a terminal with the claude CLI
Run this from the game folder:

claude mcp add --transport http higgsfield https://mcp.higgsfield.ai
Then start claude in that terminal and type /mcp. Pick higgsfield and choose to authenticate, which opens the Higgsfield sign-in page. The /mcp step only works in a terminal claude session, not in this app window.

Either way, start a new session afterwards so the Higgsfield tools load. Then tell me what to make, and I'll say what it will cost before spending credits.

how

Click in Remote MCP server URL and type https://mcp.higgsfield.ai/mcp. If it won't connect, try https://mcp.higgsfield.ai, which is the address Higgsfield's help page gives.
Leave Advanced settings and the OAuth fields blank. Higgsfield handles sign-in itself.
Click Add, then Connect, and sign in to Higgsfield when its page opens.
This window says "Connect Supercomputer to your data and tools", so it's a different app, not Claude. Adding Higgsfield there gives that app access, not me. Checking which 3D models Higgsfield offers and what they take as input:
Used higgsfield: Explore Models
Higgsfield does much more than images. What your credits can buy for the game:

* 3D models: from a text prompt, from one picture, or from 2–4 photos of the same thing. Out comes a GLB file Godot loads directly, with optional textures and material maps.
* Rigging and animation: a humanoid model gets a skeleton, and there's a library of about 700 ready-made moves (idle, walk, run and so on). There's also re-meshing to a lower polygon count and re-texturing an existing model.
* Images, video, voices and sound.

Getting the most for the credits: go image first, then 3D. A picture is cheap, and you can reject it for next to nothing. Only a picture you approve gets turned into a model. That's also the most reliable route, since text straight to 3D is the gamble. I'd keep models low-poly (10–30k triangles) so they don't hurt the frame rate I measured last night.
What the game needs, where a model replaces a stand-in:

1. Hornee from your own photos. You asked for Hornee as a 3D model rebuilt from your photos. Multi-photo to 3D does exactly that, using your plush rather than generated imagery.
2. Items you carry and hold. The checklist wants a model per item instead of a name in a list: the BREACH NINE gun, the breach ram, the Black Mirror phone, the shiv, the restraint. Most of these are drawn from boxes right now.
3. Lab set pieces: the grown bodies in the vats, the surgical lamp and drill, CCTV cameras.
4. The examiner, rigged so he can walk and gesture. Your notes say to keep the stand-in until you call the M1 sheet final, so this waits for you.

What I'd hold back on:

* Video, which is the most expensive.
* Sound, since the game's sound language is still your open question.
* Anything generated from your reference clips, which stay mood only.

First step, to learn real prices: the tools don't show costs, so I'd do one test pair: one image of the BREACH NINE gun, then a cheap untextured model of it. I check your balance after each step, which gives the real cost of both, and you see the model in Godot before we spend more.

I found why the sword breaks in third person, and I've split the fix between Codex and me.

Why it breaks: the sword is driven entirely by mouse movement. Which side you swing from, how fast, and how committed the swing is all come from how you move the mouse. In third person the mouse turns the camera instead, so every camera turn gets read as a sword swing. The sandbox has a second problem: V only changes a setting. There's no third-person camera and no player body there, so it never actually leaves first person.

The "dodge" in both the sandbox and the Hunt is a 0.28-second slide. The body leans slightly and there's no roll.

The fix, Souls-style: first person keeps mouse-drag swings. Third person gets set attacks triggered by buttons and aimed by where you're moving or by your lock-on, never by the mouse. On top of that, a proper roll with a short invulnerability window and a stamina cost.
